rv.q: Josie Rourke’s production is ferocious but light on its feet.
It’s a play that confirms Chetin-Leuner as a clear-sighted yet sanguine chronicler of all manner of relationships, not least with ourselves.
Sophia Chitin-Leuner's unsettling new play about porn is a ground-breaker - not least because it dares to be funny, as well as deeply disturbing.
Anchored by Mod, Porn Play is by turns funny and disturbing – a welcome and bold addition to the growing discourse surrounding sex and the internet.
This is an uneven but bold probing of a dirty little secret in society that finds, in Ambika Mod, an eloquent expression of underlying pain.
This new play... is a mess of provocations, as elliptical and frustrating as it is sparky and inquisitive... but for all its nebulous muddle, in Josie Rourke’s striking production, it compels.

It’s a bold play with a fantastically committed performance from Mod.
Porn Play operates on a broader canvas but delivers a portrait of a woman who remains more symbol than substance.
Sophia Chetin-Leuner has written a brave play on a difficult subject: pornography.
The funny and unsettling new production, Porn Play, makes its world premiere at the Royal Court Theatre, starring Ambika Mod (This is Going to Hurt, One Day).
Mod and the others turn a rather superficial script into a show that, for all its defects, is worth seeing.

Despite the fine acting, Chetin-Leuner has little new or valuable to say about her eye-catching subject that hasn't already been well covered by the likes of Steve McQueen's 2011 sex addiction drama Shame.
But mostly this is an absorbing, witty, layered play: and Chetin-Leuner nails Milton and Eve as singular metaphors. A must-see.
I left Porn Play feeling incredibly satisfied by what I had witnessed, with not a drop of regret.
Porn Play is a timely and involving show, with a fine young cast, and an author with fresh, compelling perspectives to offer.
Porn Play is an interesting watch that made me not just think, but read the whole playtext through.
The performances are unflinching, and its staging is creative, but in lacking clarity in its narrative and messaging, the same can’t be said for Porn Play’s script.
The gradual and drastic erosion of Ani’s sense of self culminates in a brutally sad climax in a powerful production that forces this taboo subject into the spotlight.

Chetin-Leuner establishes an engaging premise and delivers it with adequate deftness. Overall, the script is crafted with upbeat pacing, sharp dialogue, and perceptiveness. The text overflows (smirk) with interesting analysis of society’s codes and their understanding of relationships, love, and desire.
The play is both too much and too little.

cn.t: Ambika Mod delivers a fearless performance in this bold but uneven exploration of pornography addiction that divides critics with its provocative subject matter and striking staging, though many find the script frustratingly distant.

vr.q: Pawn Play is a play well worth seeing for its moving, insightful look at pornography's effect on sex and relationships.
